title: Local jan-san (janitorial & sanitation) distributor for Chicago-area facilities
subindustry: Janitorial/sanitation paper, liners, chemicals, dispensers, equipment
product_service: Recurring supply of can liners, towel/tissue, hand soap, floor and restroom chemicals, dispensers, mops/carts and small floor machines, delivered on scheduled routes; optional dispenser conversion programs and chemical-dilution system installs.
target_customer: Building service contractors (BSCs), property managers of offices/industrial parks, private schools and churches, light-industrial plants, auto dealers, non-acute healthcare in Chicago metro; 1-100 sites each.
purchase_motivation: Consumables they cannot run out of; labor savings from dilution systems; one-stop consolidated delivery; slow/unreliable service from consolidated incumbents.
spending_evidence: Paper & paper products merchant wholesalers (incl. jan-san paper) generated ~$103B sales at 23.9% gross margin in 2022 [C, WS16-S018]; consolidators Bunzl (GBP 11.8bn revenue) and Imperial Dade (230+ locations) are built on this spend [A/B, WS16-S030, WS16-S032].
representative_operators: Imperial Dade / BradyIFS (imperialbrady.com) — 13k+ associates, 230+ locations [B, WS16-S032]
Bunzl plc — 220-230+ acquisitions since 2004, operating margin 7.7% [A, WS16-S030, WS16-S031]
Essendant — two-step wholesaler supplying small jan-san resellers, Lincolnshire IL [B, WS16-S029]
revenue_mechanism: Buy-resell markup on consumables; equipment sales; occasional service/repair of floor machines.
typical_transaction_value: $300-$3,000 per delivery; small BSC accounts $10k-$60k/yr; multi-site accounts $100k+/yr [E]
direct_costs: Product COGS, delivery (van/driver or LTL), freight-in, rebates net of buying-group fees, dispenser placement capex.
contribution_profit_note: Incumbent industry implied pre-tax operating margin ~6% for paper/packaging wholesalers (GM 23.9% minus opex ~17.7%) [C, WS16-S019]; new entrant lacks rebates/volume pricing so expect 4-6 pts lower GM at start [E].
working_capital_note: Net-30 receivables from commercial accounts (BSCs often pay slow); starter inventory $10-40k unless drop-shipping via two-step wholesaler; supplier credit after credit application (Essendant can approve in days) [B, WS16-S028]; dispenser programs tie up capital until recouped.
sales_cycle: 2-8 weeks for small accounts (trial order, price comparison); 3-6 months for multi-site BSCs/property managers.
repeat_purchase: consumable-replenishment — weekly/monthly reorders; dispenser placements lock in towel/soap refills
acquisition_channels: Door-to-door/field sales to BSCs and property managers
Cleaning contractor associations and local BSC networks
customer_accessibility: Buyers numerous and identifiable (BSCs, facility managers); purchasing is relationship + price driven; many accounts tied to consolidated distributors via contracts or dispenser placements.
supplier_accessibility: Assumed/partly confirmed: two-step wholesaler (Essendant) sells to resellers meeting volume minimum + resale certificate [B, WS16-S028]; buying groups (AFFLINK etc.) admit independent distributors but criteria not published but publish no criteria or fees [B, WS16-S042]; brand-level authorization varies (e.g., Rubbermaid online reseller controls) [B, WS16-S033].
competitive_intensity: high — national consolidators, Amazon Business, Staples/ODP, Grainger, plus entrenched local independents
entry_strategy: Service wedge in a dense geography: guaranteed next-day delivery, dispenser conversion + dilution-control installs, consolidated billing, and targeting BSCs underserved after consolidator acquisitions; plan exit/roll-up potential since consolidators acquire local houses.
licenses: Illinois business registration (Secretary of State LLC filing) and IDOR registration (Form REG-1) to collect ROT and issue resale certificates (CRT-61) [A, WS16-S036]; general liability/product liability insurance; no professional license; USDOT/hazmat awareness for transporting limited-quantity cleaning chemicals (MISSING detail)
regulatory_barriers: Low. SDS/GHS labeling compliance for chemicals; green-certified product requirements in some public contracts.
operational_risks: Delivery reliability, stockouts, driver turnover, dispenser loss, price wars on paper.
financial_risks: Thin margins; paper/resin price swings; customer concentration on a few BSCs; bad debt from small contractors.
geographic_constraints: Route density matters: Chicago metro first; each new metro needs a branch or 3PL.
founder_expertise: Product knowledge (chemistry dilution, paper specs), pricing, purchasing, route logistics; ISSA-type training.
staffing: Year 1: founder + part-time driver; Year 2: inside CSR/purchasing, 1-2 outside reps; warehouse lead by $1.5M revenue.
automation_potential: AI-assisted quoting and order entry, reorder prediction per account, route optimization, invoice/AR follow-up; delivery and field selling stay human.
delegation_potential: Good — distribution roles (driver, CSR, buyer, outside rep) have an established labor market.
scalability: Moderate: branch replication and tuck-ins; consolidators prove scale but at ~7-8% operating margin [A, WS16-S030].
expansion: Floor-machine dealership/service (WS16-020), foodservice disposables (WS16-002), PPE (WS16-004), facility packaging (WS16-003); sell to a consolidator.
roic_note: At ~$2M revenue: receivables ~$165k + inventory ~$120k + van/dispensers ~$40k less payables ~$100k ≈ $225k invested for ~$80-120k operating profit ≈ 35-55% [E]; drop-ship start improves early ROIC.
critical_assumptions: A newcomer can buy at competitive cost via two-step wholesaler/buying group within 6-12 months
Service wedge wins BSC accounts despite consolidator pricing
unanswered_questions: Buying-group (AFFLINK, Network Services) admission criteria and fees
Essendant minimum annual purchase volume and drop-ship fees
Number of independent jan-san distributors in Chicago metro (CBP NAICS 423850 by county)
Typical jan-san small-distributor gross margin (ISSA benchmarks inaccessible — 403)
failure_modes: Price-only competition against consolidators erodes GM below 20%
Too few accounts per route; delivery cost swamps margin
Over-stocking inventory and slow-paying BSCs drain cash
Key account acquired by a national BSC that switches to national contract
score_rationale: fcf 4: realistic yr-3 $30-150k on ~$1.5-2.5M revenue at incumbent-like 5-7% margins. roic 4: inventory+AR heavy. resilience 7: essential consumables. entry 4: crowded with consolidators; service wedge copyable. feasibility 9: no license beyond tax registration.
preliminary_verdict: advance — conventional, recession-resilient consumables distribution with a documented exit market, but thin margins; good benchmark candidate for screening.

title: Foodservice disposables & custom-printed packaging distributor for independent restaurants
subindustry: Foodservice disposables (to-go containers, cups, bags) and custom-printed packaging
product_service: Stock to-go containers, cups, lids, bags, gloves and cleaning supplies plus small-MOQ custom-printed cups/bags/boxes sourced from domestic converters or Asian factories for independent cafes, bubble-tea shops, bakeries, ghost kitchens.
target_customer: Owner-operators of independent restaurants, cafes, bakeries, caterers and small chains (1-20 units) in Chicago metro.
purchase_motivation: Continuous consumable need; branded packaging as marketing; frustration with broadline minimums and cash-and-carry trips.
spending_evidence: Broadline foodservice distribution (Sysco $84.5B revenue, GM 18.5%) and not-for-resale consumables (Bunzl) document the spend [A, WS16-S016, WS16-S030]; paper/packaging wholesalers GM 23.9% [C, WS16-S018].
representative_operators: Sysco/US Foods broadline (disposables as add-on) [A, WS16-S016]
revenue_mechanism: Markup on stock disposables; higher markup on custom-printed runs (deposit-funded).
typical_transaction_value: $200-$1,500 per stock order biweekly; custom print runs $1,500-$15,000 [E]
direct_costs: Product, freight (bulky/cube-heavy), import duties on Asian-sourced items, delivery labor.
contribution_profit_note: Stock disposables are cube-heavy and price-shopped: likely 15-22% GM; custom print 25-40% GM but lumpy [E].
working_capital_note: Restaurants often pay COD/card (good); custom imports need 30-50% factory deposits 60-90 days before delivery; bulky inventory needs warehouse space.
sales_cycle: Days to weeks (owner decides); custom print 2-6 weeks.
acquisition_channels: Restaurant supply and equipment dealers referrals
customer_accessibility: Very reachable (thousands of independents in Chicago), but high churn and price shopping; restaurant failure rate high.
supplier_accessibility: Assumed: major disposables makers sell through distributors; custom printers/Asian factories open to small importers; brand authorizations not verified.
competitive_intensity: extreme — broadline distributors, cash-and-carry, Amazon/WebstaurantStore, consolidators
entry_strategy: Small-MOQ custom-branded packaging with fast design mockups plus reliable stock delivery bundled; target segments broadliners under-serve (boba, specialty coffee, bakeries).
licenses: Illinois business registration (Secretary of State LLC filing) and IDOR registration (Form REG-1) to collect ROT and issue resale certificates (CRT-61) [A, WS16-S036]; general liability/product liability insurance; no professional license; importer of record obligations (customs bond via broker) if importing; local packaging rules (PFAS/plastic restrictions — Illinois status MISSING)
regulatory_barriers: Food-contact material compliance; evolving PFAS/polystyrene bans in some jurisdictions (Illinois specifics unverified).
operational_risks: Warehouse space for bulky goods; custom print errors; long import lead times.
financial_risks: Tariffs on imported disposables (IEEPA tariffs struck down Feb 2026 but replaced under other authorities) [A, WS16-S022, WS16-S021]; restaurant bad debt; thin stock margins.
geographic_constraints: Local delivery density for stock; custom print can ship nationally.
founder_expertise: Packaging specs, sourcing/import process, restaurant sales.
staffing: Founder + driver; design/CSR hire by year 2.
automation_potential: AI mockup generation for custom print, quoting, reorder reminders; sales and delivery human.
delegation_potential: Moderate — standard distribution roles; custom sourcing judgment harder to delegate.
scalability: Moderate locally; custom-print e-commerce can scale nationally but competes with many online printers.
expansion: Jan-san (WS16-001), specialty food ingredients (WS16-027), national e-commerce custom-packaging.
roic_note: Low capital if COD customers, but bulky inventory and import deposits; operating margins likely 3-6% on stock goods [E].
critical_assumptions: Restaurants switch from cash-and-carry for delivery convenience
unanswered_questions: Actual small-distributor margins on foodservice disposables
Minimum order terms from domestic custom-print converters
score_rationale: fcf 3: thin margins and high churn. access 6: owners easy to reach and decide fast. entry 3: extreme competition. resilience 6: consumable but restaurant sector cyclical.
preliminary_verdict: hold — reachable buyers but commodity margins; only the custom-print niche is interesting and is closer to a sourcing broker.

title: Industrial & warehouse packaging distributor (stretch film, corrugated, tape, equipment service) for Chicago logistics/manufacturing
subindustry: Industrial packaging supplies and packaging equipment
product_service: Stretch film, corrugated boxes (stock and custom), carton-sealing tape, void fill, strapping, labels, plus placement and service of stretch wrappers and case sealers; packaging-cost audits.
target_customer: Operations/purchasing managers at 3PL warehouses, e-commerce fulfillment centers, food and light manufacturers in the Chicago/I-55/I-80 corridors (10-500 employees).
purchase_motivation: Continuous consumable usage; downtime cost if packaging runs out; cost-per-load savings from film/equipment optimization.
spending_evidence: Paper & packaging merchant wholesalers: 23.9% GM, ~6% implied operating margin (2022) [C, WS16-S018, WS16-S019]; consolidator Imperial Dade includes industrial packaging [B, WS16-S032]; manufacturer IPG runs a distributor B2B portal [B, WS16-S045].
representative_operators: Uline (catalog direct; private, figures not sourced)
Imperial Dade / BradyIFS industrial packaging [B, WS16-S032]
revenue_mechanism: Markup on consumables; equipment sales/rental; service calls; custom box margin.
typical_transaction_value: $1,000-$10,000 per monthly order for a mid-size warehouse; equipment $8k-$40k [E]
direct_costs: Product COGS (resin-linked film, corrugated), freight-in, delivery, equipment technician labor.
contribution_profit_note: Industry average ~6% pre-tax margin [C, WS16-S019]; equipment-service accounts stickier and higher margin [E].
working_capital_note: Net-30 to net-60 customer terms (3PLs push long terms); inventory of film/corrugated bulky; manufacturers may drop-ship truckloads to large users.
sales_cycle: 1-3 months (trial on one line, cost-per-load test).
acquisition_channels: Field sales to warehouses in industrial parks
customer_accessibility: Good — Chicago is a dense logistics market; facilities identifiable via public lease/industrial data; buyers open to cost-saving trials.
supplier_accessibility: Partly confirmed: tape/film maker IPG sells via distributors (distributor portal) [B, WS16-S045]; buying groups recruit independents but publish no criteria [B, WS16-S042]; credit terms for new distributor unknown.
competitive_intensity: high — Uline catalog, national consolidators, many local independents
entry_strategy: Cost-per-load engineering (downgauged film + equipment tuning) with guaranteed savings, fast local delivery and equipment repair; Uline can't do on-site optimization.
licenses: Illinois business registration (Secretary of State LLC filing) and IDOR registration (Form REG-1) to collect ROT and issue resale certificates (CRT-61) [A, WS16-S036]; general liability/product liability insurance; no professional license
operational_risks: Equipment technician availability; resin price spikes; delivery logistics for bulky goods.
financial_risks: Customer concentration on a few large warehouses; long receivables; tariff effects on imported tape/equipment [A, WS16-S021, WS16-S022].
geographic_constraints: Local density; Chicago logistics corridors favorable.
founder_expertise: Packaging materials science (film gauges, ECT/burst ratings), equipment basics; founder's technical/research background is a plus.
staffing: Founder + driver; equipment tech by year 2; inside CSR.
automation_potential: Spec comparison, quote generation, reorder forecasting from usage; equipment service is human.
delegation_potential: Good — standard distribution and technician roles.
scalability: Moderate: replicate in other logistics hubs; add custom corrugated brokerage.
expansion: Jan-san for same facilities (WS16-001), AIDC labels (WS16-011), racking (WS16-018), safety (WS16-004).
roic_note: Similar to jan-san: ~$200-300k invested at $2M revenue for $80-150k operating profit (30-60%) [E].
critical_assumptions: Savings-led selling wins trials vs Uline
Supplier pricing for a new distributor allows ≥20% GM
unanswered_questions: Packaging distributor buying groups and admission criteria
Manufacturer minimums for direct accounts (film, tape)
Chicago-area count of independent packaging distributors
failure_modes: Large customer moves to national contract
Bulky inventory and slow pay drain cash
score_rationale: access 6: dense, identifiable warehouse buyers with measurable savings pitch. resilience 6: consumable but tied to industrial/e-commerce volumes. entry 4: crowded; engineering wedge helps. feasibility 10: no license.
preliminary_verdict: advance — consumable replenishment in a dense Chicago logistics market with a technical savings wedge; margins thin but real.

title: Safety/PPE specialty distributor with services (fit testing, gas-detector calibration/rental) for contractors and plants
product_service: Gloves, hi-vis, eye/hearing protection, fall protection, respirators, first-aid; plus respirator fit testing, gas-detector bump/calibration and rental, fall-protection inspection, and site vending/VMI for small plants.
target_customer: Safety managers/superintendents at contractors (construction, utilities, demolition) and plant managers at 20-500 employee manufacturers in Illinois.
purchase_motivation: OSHA-driven compliance, injury cost, jobsite downtime; consumable usage.
spending_evidence: Scale MRO/safety incumbents: Grainger GM 39.1%/op 13.9%, Fastenal 45.0%/20.2%, MSC 40.9%/8.0% (FY2025-26) [A, WS16-S002, WS16-S001, WS16-S003]; supplier Ergodyne sets a $75,000/yr minimum for direct distributors [B, WS16-S038].
revenue_mechanism: Markup on PPE consumables; service fees (fit tests, calibration); rental fees for detectors.
typical_transaction_value: $500-$5,000 monthly per contractor account; fit test $30-$75/person; detector rental $X/week (MISSING) [E]
direct_costs: Product COGS; technician time; calibration gas; vending machine capex.
contribution_profit_note: Incumbents achieve 39-45% GM with scale purchasing and private label [A]; new entrant 25-35% blended with services [E].
working_capital_note: Net-30 commercial terms; contractors slow-pay (45-60 days common, E); inventory of sizes/SKUs; rental fleet capital.
sales_cycle: 2-8 weeks; master contracts with larger contractors 3-6 months.
customer_accessibility: Good — contractors identifiable via permits and public bids; safety managers welcome compliance help.
supplier_accessibility: Partly confirmed: Ergodyne requires $75k annual sales to buy direct, else routes to authorized wholesaler [B, WS16-S038]; other brand terms MISSING.
competitive_intensity: high — Grainger, Fastenal, Amazon Business and independents
entry_strategy: Service-led: compliance services (fit testing, detector calibration, inspection logs) that national catalogs don't perform on site; bundle PPE supply.
licenses: Illinois business registration (Secretary of State LLC filing) and IDOR registration (Form REG-1) to collect ROT and issue resale certificates (CRT-61) [A, WS16-S036]; general liability/product liability insurance; no professional license; fit-testing competency (no state license; OSHA 1910.134 protocol) and calibration training from detector OEMs (assumed)
regulatory_barriers: Low; liability exposure for inspection services.
operational_risks: Technician capacity; SKU proliferation (sizes); vending maintenance.
financial_risks: Tariffs on imported gloves/apparel (IEEPA struck Feb 2026, replaced) [A, WS16-S022, WS16-S021]; construction cyclicality; bad debt.
founder_expertise: OSHA standards, PPE specs, gas-detection; selling to contractors.
staffing: Founder + safety technician by year 1-2; driver/CSR.
automation_potential: Compliance record-keeping, reminders, quoting, SKU-matching; services human.
roic_note: Inventory + rental fleet + AR ≈ $150-250k at scale for ~$80-150k profit [E].
critical_assumptions: Services wedge differentiates vs catalog pricing
Supplier access via wholesaler at ≥25% GM
score_rationale: access 6: identifiable buyers, compliance-led pitch. entry 4: incumbents strong; services wedge moderate. resilience 6: compliance demand but construction cyclical.
preliminary_verdict: hold — viable service-plus-supply model, but overlaps heavily with scale MRO incumbents; screen against WS05/WS03 service plays.

title: Lab supplies distributor for biotech startups and academic labs (Chicago/Illinois)
product_service: Pipette tips, tubes, plates, gloves, chemicals/reagents (non-controlled), small benchtop equipment; same-day local delivery; private-label equivalents.
target_customer: Lab managers/PIs at biotech startups (Fulton Market, incubators), university labs, hospital research labs, contract labs.
purchase_motivation: Continuous consumable usage; price; availability during supply shortages; speed.
spending_evidence: Avantor (VWR) $6.55B revenue, GM 32.7%, ex-impairment operating margin ~8% [A, WS16-S010, WS16-S037]; customers sticky — ~45% of Avantor sales from 15+-year relationships [A, WS16-S037].
representative_operators: Smaller independents e.g., Thomas Scientific (private; not sourced)
revenue_mechanism: Markup on consumables; private-label higher margin.
direct_costs: Product COGS; cold-chain shipping for some reagents; small inventory.
contribution_profit_note: Universities buy through negotiated contracts/punch-out catalogs; startups price-shop Amazon/Fisher. New-entrant margin likely low on branded goods [E].
working_capital_note: University AP slow (45-60 days typical, E); inventory for same-day promise.
sales_cycle: Startups: weeks; universities: vendor onboarding/contract months.
customer_accessibility: Moderate-low: universities locked into Fisher/VWR contracts and procurement systems; startups few and price-sensitive.
supplier_accessibility: Unknown: major brands sell via Fisher/VWR or selective distributors; private-label sourcing from Asian manufacturers feasible but quality validation needed.
competitive_intensity: high — two dominant distributors plus Amazon
entry_strategy: Private-label consumables with documented equivalence + same-day delivery to incubator clusters.
licenses: Illinois business registration (Secretary of State LLC filing) and IDOR registration (Form REG-1) to collect ROT and issue resale certificates (CRT-61) [A, WS16-S036]; general liability/product liability insurance; no professional license; hazardous material shipping for some chemicals; no DEA unless controlled substances (avoid)
operational_risks: Quality complaints on private label; cold chain.
financial_risks: Biotech funding cycles (startup demand volatile); tariffs on imported plastics.
geographic_constraints: Chicago biotech cluster small vs Boston/SF.
founder_expertise: Founder's research background is a genuine asset (knows lab workflows).
scalability: Limited locally; national e-commerce private label possible.
expansion: Lab equipment refurbishment (WS04), private-label consumables e-commerce.
roic_note: Inventory + AR moderate; margins compressed by incumbents [E].
unanswered_questions: University procurement openness to small vendors (E&I contracts)
score_rationale: access 3: procurement contracts and entrenched duopoly. entry 3: weak wedge. founder fit is the only plus.
preliminary_verdict: hold — founder-fit is good but buyers are locked into Fisher/VWR; refer to WS04 lab consumables.

title: Promotional products / branded merchandise distributor (ASI/PPAI supplier network, supplier-decorated drop-ship)
product_service: Branded apparel, drinkware, bags, tech accessories, trade-show items, employee gifts and online company stores, sourced from 3,000+ suppliers who decorate and drop-ship to the client.
target_customer: Marketing, HR and event managers at SMBs and mid-market companies, schools, nonprofits, associations.
purchase_motivation: Brand visibility, events, employee recognition/onboarding, client gifts.
spending_evidence: ASI cites a $27.7B industry with 3,000+ suppliers and 1.2M+ products [C, WS16-S026]; ASI testimonial of a member growing to $16M revenue in 11 years [D, WS16-S026].
representative_operators: ASI testimonial firm (Whitestone) — ~$16M revenue, ~50 staff after 11 years [D, WS16-S026]
Large distributors e.g., 4imprint, HALO, BAMKO (not sourced)
Tens of thousands of small distributors (count MISSING)
revenue_mechanism: Markup on supplier 'coded' wholesale pricing; setup/decoration pass-through; company-store management fees.
direct_costs: Supplier product + decoration, freight, samples, payment fees; commissioned rep splits if using reps.
contribution_profit_note: ASI states average 37% gross margin [C, WS16-S026] and elsewhere ~40% [D, WS16-S027] (discrepancy kept); independent reps commonly take a share of gross profit (rate MISSING).
working_capital_note: No inventory (made to order) [C, WS16-S026]; client deposits common (assumed); supplier terms net-30 after credit, else prepay (assumed); net-30 corporate receivables.
repeat_purchase: occasional to recurring — events, onboarding kits, company stores
customer_accessibility: Every organization is a buyer and identifiable; but heavy competition and price comparison.
supplier_accessibility: Confirmed open: ASI membership gives same-day sourcing access to 3,000+ suppliers; 'no experience required' [C, WS16-S026].
competitive_intensity: extreme — very low barriers, many small distributors, online players
entry_strategy: Vertical specialization (e.g., construction/manufacturing onboarding kits, healthcare systems) and managed company stores that create recurring programs.
licenses: Illinois business registration (Secretary of State LLC filing) and IDOR registration (Form REG-1) to collect ROT and issue resale certificates (CRT-61) [A, WS16-S036]; general liability/product liability insurance; no professional license; ASI/PPAI/SAGE membership (fee MISSING)
regulatory_barriers: Low (product safety/CPSIA for youth items, Prop 65 for CA shipments).
operational_risks: Order errors, decoration quality, deadlines.
financial_risks: Discretionary marketing spend falls in recessions; tariffs raise imported hard-goods costs [A, WS16-S022].
founder_expertise: Selling, project management, product knowledge; easy to learn.
staffing: Founder sells; account coordinator by ~$500k sales; commissioned reps.
automation_potential: AI mockups, product search, quoting, order tracking; relationship selling human.
delegation_potential: Good — rep-based model common in industry.
scalability: Moderate — scales via reps and programs; ASI testimonial shows $16M possible.
roic_note: Capital at risk <$15k plus founder time; operating profit/capital very high if deposits fund supplier payments [E].
unanswered_questions: Supplier credit terms for new distributors
failure_modes: Dependency on one or two big clients
score_rationale: roic 8: near-zero capital, made-to-order drop-ship. access 6: buyers everywhere. entry 3: extreme competition. resilience 4: discretionary. feasibility 10.
preliminary_verdict: advance — lowest-capital, fastest-to-revenue distribution model found; economics depend on sales execution and specialization.

title: Independent manufacturers' rep agency — electronic components & embedded/industrial electronics (Midwest OEM territory)
product_service: Outsourced field sales for several non-competing component/module makers (connectors, power supplies, sensors, embedded modules): design-in support with OEM engineers, quoting, and account management; commissions on resulting production shipments including through franchised distributors (POS).
target_customer: Principals: small-to-mid component manufacturers lacking Midwest coverage. Customers: design engineers and buyers at Illinois/Wisconsin/Indiana OEMs (industrial controls, medical devices, ag/heavy equipment, appliances).
purchase_motivation: Principals pay variable-cost sales coverage instead of fixed direct reps; OEMs value technical help and multi-line access.
spending_evidence: Wholesale agents & brokers earned $34.2B commissions on $765B of sales in 2022 = 4.5% average realized commission [C, WS16-S020]; MANA's rate surveys stopped in 2005 and are member-gated [C, WS16-S024].
representative_operators: Many regional rep firms (names/revenues not sourced)
MANA illustrative firm: $10M principal sales → ~$500k commissions, owner keeps ~$152k [D, WS16-S023]
revenue_mechanism: % commission on principal's invoiced sales into territory (often split between design-win and ship-to territories).
typical_transaction_value: Production program $50k-$2M/yr per OEM part; commission ~3-6% of that (rate for electronics MISSING; 4.5% all-agent average) [C/E]
direct_costs: Travel, samples/demo kits, CRM, salaried/commissioned sub-reps (MANA illustration: ~61% of commission to payroll) [D, WS16-S023].
contribution_profit_note: Commission income is ~100% gross margin; owner retains ~30% of commission income in MANA's illustrative 3-person firm [D, WS16-S023].
working_capital_note: No inventory/AR on goods; commissions paid after principal invoices/collects (often monthly, 30-60 days lag, E); design-win revenue arrives 6-24 months after first call → founder must self-fund living costs.
sales_cycle: Design-in 6-24 months; signing a line 1-3 months.
repeat_purchase: recurring-contract — commissions recur for life of program while line held
acquisition_channels: Direct outreach to manufacturers lacking Midwest coverage
customer_accessibility: OEM engineers reachable but sales cycles very long; principals readily sign new reps for uncovered territories but give weak/unknown lines to unproven agencies.
supplier_accessibility: Assumed: manufacturers recruit reps via MANA/ERA listings; terms are negotiable; top lines held by incumbents for decades.
competitive_intensity: moderate — incumbent agencies own best lines; distributors' FAEs and direct sales compete
entry_strategy: Technical credibility (founder's engineering/research background) + focus on startup/emerging component makers (incl. tariff-driven new US/Mexico suppliers) that incumbents ignore.
licenses: Illinois LLC + IDOR registration only if taking title to goods; commission-only agencies hold no inventory. Illinois Sales Representative Act (820 ILCS 120) governs commission payment on termination — exists per analyst knowledge, text NOT verified this session (ilga.gov unreachable)
regulatory_barriers: Low; export-control awareness for some components.
operational_risks: Line termination once territory is developed; house-account carve-outs; commission disputes.
financial_risks: Long unpaid ramp; electronics cyclicality; principal insolvency.
founder_expertise: Electronics engineering basics, design-cycle selling, contract negotiation.
staffing: Founder alone for 1-2 yrs; add outside rep and inside support once commissions exceed ~$300k.
automation_potential: Prospect research on OEM programs, quote prep, CRM hygiene, POS report reconciliation; engineering relationships human.
delegation_potential: Moderate — rep firms hire sub-reps but principals value principal-owner relationship.
scalability: Limited by territory and lines; agencies of 5-20 people common (count MISSING).
expansion: Stocking/buy-sell for small principals; adjacent territories; acquiring retiring agencies later.
roic_note: Capital is mostly founder time and living costs; once lines produce, operating profit/capital is very high, but ramp is 1-3 years [E].
critical_assumptions: Can sign 5-8 viable lines within 12 months
Design wins convert to production within 18-24 months
unanswered_questions: Electronics-specific commission rates (ERA data not accessed)
Number of rep firms in IL (CBP 425120)
score_rationale: roic 7: near-zero capital but long ramp. access 4: long design cycles and credibility wall. entry 5: relationships accumulate into moat but lines can be pulled. feasibility 10.
preliminary_verdict: hold — asset-light with good founder fit, but 18-24-month ramp and line-termination risk make yr-3 FCF unreliable.

title: Foodservice equipment & supplies (FES) rep agency calling on dealers, consultants and chains
product_service: Territory sales representation for commercial kitchen equipment and smallwares makers: dealer training, consultant/spec calls, chain-account support, test kitchen demos.
target_customer: Principals: FES manufacturers. Customers: foodservice equipment dealers, design consultants, multi-unit restaurant chains, institutions (schools, hospitals).
purchase_motivation: Manufacturers outsource regional coverage; dealers rely on reps for specs, quotes and service coordination.

operational_risks: Technical support capability; label print quality issues.

Number of AIDC VARs in Chicago

preliminary_verdict: advance — technical founder fit plus recurring consumables; worth screening against packaging/racking plays.

title: Niche B2B e-commerce store using manufacturer drop-ship, stocking only proven SKUs (Global Industrial playbook in a vertical)
subindustry: Vertical B2B catalog (e.g., lab/school furniture, material handling, signage, facility equipment)
product_service: A specialized online catalog for one vertical (e.g., cleanroom/lab furniture, industrial carts and lockers, facility safety signage) with expert content, quoting, and vendor drop-ship; stocks fast movers after they prove velocity.
target_customer: Purchasing managers, facility managers and small-business owners searching online; schools/municipalities via cooperative contracts later.

direct_costs: Product, drop-ship fees, freight (LTL for bulky items), payment fees, Google/Bing ads.

working_capital_note: Customers pay by card/PO; suppliers drop-ship on net-30 after credit approval (assumed) → can be cash-positive; stocking later.
customer_accessibility: Buyers actively search online — but traffic costs money and incumbents dominate SEO.
supplier_accessibility: Mixed: many manufacturers drop-ship for dealers; major brands gate online resellers and enforce MAP (Rubbermaid policy) [B, WS16-S033].

operational_risks: Freight damage claims, vendor stockouts, returns of bulky items.
financial_risks: Ad-cost inflation; MAP compression; platform/algorithm dependence.
founder_expertise: E-commerce, SEO/ads, catalog data — founder's tech skills fit.
automation_potential: Catalog enrichment, spec Q&A, quote generation, customer service drafting — meaningful and cheap post-2026.
expansion: Stocking proven SKUs; private label (WS16-014); government contracts (WS08).

critical_assumptions: Vertical has drop-ship-friendly manufacturers without strict online gating
unanswered_questions: Conversion rates for niche B2B sites
score_rationale: cash 7: card/PO + drop-ship. ai 7: catalog/content/CS automation real. entry 3: heavy incumbents and Amazon. resilience 4: ad-platform dependence.
preliminary_verdict: hold — capital-light, documented playbook, but CAC and brand gating make new-entrant economics speculative.
